title: 28 February 2026 U.S. decision to launch Operation Epic Fury against Iran

decision_cutoff.date_or_period: Immediately before U.S. combat operations began on 28 February 2026
decision_cutoff.definition: The U.S. decision whether to launch broad strikes in Iran, alongside Israel, against nuclear, missile, naval and other regime/military capabilities while citing an imminent nuclear/security threat and self-defence rationale.

live_conflict_note: This case is frozen before the first 2026 strikes. Later Iranian retaliation, campaign duration, casualties, costs and later intelligence/legal statements are reveal material only.

packets.masking_note: Names the United States, Iran, Operation Epic Fury and the public pre-strike evidence.
Names removed; preserves nuclear-safeguards gap, prior ceasefire, missile/proxy threat, active diplomacy, broad strike objectives and uncertainty over weaponisation/imminence.

expected_constitutional_constraints: A serious nuclear-proliferation risk is morally relevant but is not identical to evidence of an authorised or imminent nuclear attack.
When broad preventive force is justified by imminence, the evidential burden for imminence must rise with the scale and irreversibility of the proposed attack.
The evaluator must preserve the distinction between IAEA inability to verify material, high enrichment capability and an actual political decision to build/use a weapon.
Iran's demonstrated missile, proxy and prior retaliatory capabilities are real security evidence and must not be minimised.
Active diplomatic progress immediately before attack is relevant to whether non-military alternatives were genuinely exhausted.
The 2025 U.S.-Iran direct military exchange and ceasefire are relevant context, but a prior conflict does not automatically create unlimited continuing authority for new broad attacks months later.
Nuclear sites, missile forces, naval assets and proxy-support infrastructure may present different necessity/targeting cases and should not be treated as one undifferentiated objective.

sources.citation: White House, Peace Through Strength: President Trump Launches Operation Epic Fury to Crush Iranian Regime, End Nuclear Threat
sources.use_note: States U.S. objectives and claim that diplomacy was exhausted and Iran posed an imminent nuclear/security threat. Treat those as U.S. claims requiring comparison with independent pre-strike evidence.

sources.citation: IAEA Director General report GOV/2026/8, 27 February 2026
sources.use_note: Reports no IAEA access to four declared enrichment facilities, inability to verify current inventories and last known 440.9 kg stockpile enriched up to 60% as of June 2025; calls loss of continuity a serious proliferation concern.

sources.citation: ODNI 2025 Annual Threat Assessment opening statement/report
sources.use_note: Public U.S. IC assessment stated Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and Khamenei had not authorised the suspended weapons programme, while warning of unprecedented enriched-uranium levels and missile/proxy threats. This assessment pre-dates the June 2025 war and therefore may have become stale; that uncertainty is explicit.

sources.citation: Oman Foreign Ministry, U.S.-Iran talks report significant progress and follow-on technical talks
sources.use_note: Omani mediation statement describing significant progress and planned continuation of negotiations/technical work immediately before the strikes.

sources.citation: Oman Foreign Ministry, Foreign Minister briefs U.S. Vice President on Iran talks progress
sources.use_note: Confirms diplomacy remained active one day before the attack and characterises progress as substantial/unprecedented.

sources.citation: U.S. Department of Defense, Operation Midnight Hammer briefing, June 2025
sources.use_note: Documents prior direct U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities during the 2025 Israel-Iran war.

sources.citation: Presidential statement on Iranian missile strike on Al Udeid Air Base, 23 June 2025
sources.use_note: Documents Iran's direct missile retaliation against a U.S. base and U.S. acknowledgement of advance notice/no American casualties, followed by a ceasefire context.

sources.citation: United States letter to UN Security Council under Article 51, 10 March 2026, S/2026/161
sources.use_note: Later U.S. formal self-defence justification; reveal/context only, not evidence that had to exist publicly before launch.
